title: Taking Credit
summary: My colleagues look at the debate inside the Democratic Party about which faction can take credit for the midterm romp.

Good morning. Today, I am handing it over to my colleagues.


Image


By


[Adam B. Kushner](https://www.nytimes.com/by/adam-b-kushner) and[Evan Gorelick](https://www.nytimes.com/by/evan-gorelick)


Infighting among Democrats is a historical truism, like death or taxes. And even with their nationwide midterm victories this month, there are still debates to settle. Democrats disagree with one another about tariffs, Israel, the role of fossil fuels, how much to overhaul health insurance and how much to tax the rich. (They broadly agree on data centers and the Iran war: Nobody wants those.)


Democrats looked a lot different this year than they did in recent cycles. Some torched liberal orthodoxy and ran from the right on certain issues. Others embraced socialist ideas like national health care. Most of them won. Democrats captured control of Congress and most governorships.


If defeat is an orphan, victory has many parents. Now both the moderates and the progressives agree the party’s new big-tent approach enabled its victory, even as they argue that *their* sect provided the juice. Who is right, and how divided is the party, really? After all, both factions ran — and won — mainly on affordability, a thing they agree about.


Let’s look at the arguments.


## The moderates


Moderate Democrats flipped seats in Kansas, Texas, Mississippi, South Carolina — deep-red places where the party does not typically win statewide races.


In their recruiting, party leaders prioritized candidates who could pass muster with local voters over those who lined up with the liberal orthodoxy on every (or any) issue. “None of the eight people who flipped Senate seats in Trump states ran on Bernie Sanders’s signature policies, and almost all of them ran to the right of the establishment,” Matthew Yglesias, a liberal journalist, told us, predicting a victory in Alaska.


Many of the newbies flayed the Biden administration’s immigration policy; Josh Turek of Iowa, for instance, backed a state law that made undocumented immigration a crime. James Talarico of Texas wants an “all-of-the-above” strategy for energy that still draws on fossil fuels. Annie Andrews of South Carolina said, “I don’t support biological men playing women’s sports, and I don’t support — and haven’t ever performed — gender surgery for minors.” Scott Colom of Mississippi ran on his 94 percent conviction rate as a tough-on-crime district attorney. These are not views that would have been welcomed by party leaders in 2020 or even 2024.
